newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac, Kohl, Major make joint Mideast peace plea.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Kohl, Major make joint Mideast peace plea.

text.p: The leaders of France, Britain and Germany made an unprecedented joint appeal to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Friday to meet immediately to calm violence raging in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
President Jacques Chirac, Prime Minister John Major and Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in a letter: "We are sending you a joint, solemn appeal to make the necessary calming gestures."
Chirac's office released the text in French.
The three main west European powers called for "an immediate resumption of negotiations at the highest level" and the full implementation of agreements already reached between Israel and the PLO.
"This approach appears to us to be the only way to restore calm durably in the territories and to ensure Israel's security," they said.

The leaders noted with satisfaction what they called a decision to close a controversial Israeli archeological tunnel under the Old City of Jerusalem, which sparked the outburst of violence, and called for other measures in the same spirit.
The Europeans expressed strong concern that the violence could endanger the entire Middle East peace process. At least 53 Arabs and 13 Israelis have died in three days of bloodshed.
They appealed to the statesmanship of Netanyahu and Arafat "to ensure that wisdom and peace prevail in the interest of the peoples of the region".
It was the first such joint emergency policy initiative by the European Union's "Big Three" and was issued in consultation with the EU's current Irish presidency, French officials said.
They said Chirac proposed the idea to Major and Kohl, since the three of them had played host to Netanyahu on his European tour earlier this week, just as the crisis was blowing up.
They agreed immediately and the draft texts were rapidly agreed by the three capitals. They were also in close touch with the United States, Israel's staunchest ally, the officials said.
The aim was to maximise European influence and respond to frequent complaints that the EU was too slow and powerless in reacting to crises close to its borders.

Diplomats said intensive diplomacy was under way involving the United States, the Europeans and Egypt to get Netanyahu and Arafat to meet, probably in Cairo, but both men had put conditions unacceptable to the other.

Chirac's office said he had separately called Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Arafat after the letter was sent. All three agreed on the need for urgent measures and a meeting of Netanyahu and Arafat soon.
Netanyahu accused Arafat on Friday of having cynically incited the riots and demanded that he renounce the use of violence before peace negotiations could resume.
Arafat demanded that Israel go back on the tunnel opening, and Palestinian officials said the Jewish state must also implement its delayed pullback from the West Bank city of Hebron.

Netanyahu said he would consider an invitation from Mubarak to meet Arafat in Cairo. Arafat has turned down Netanyahu's invitation to a one-to-one summit. Both men met for the first time earlier this month in Gaza.
